newsitem.title: USA: Illinois bill would restore incinerator subsidy.
newsitem.headline: Illinois bill would restore incinerator subsidy.

text.p: An Illinois lawmaker has introduced a bill that would restore a state subsidy to two bond-financed waste-to-energy incinerators.
The bill, sponsored by State Rep. Harold Murphy, D-Markham, was introduced in the General Assembly this week and is pending before the House Public Utilities Committee.

Murphy was not available to comment on the bill, which would only reinstate the subsidy for incinerators for which bonds were sold, were substantially completed and had received necessary government orders and permits.

The only two facilities that would meet that criteria are an incinerator in Robbins, financed with $320 million of bonds sold in 1994, and in Ford Heights, which was financed with $79.6 million of bonds also sold in 1994 through the Illinois Development Finance Authority.

The developers of those incinerators and two others in Fulton and Wood River that were never built are currenting fighting in court the 1996 repeal of the subsidy, which guarenteed incinerators a higher rate at which they could sell electricity they produced to utility companies. The removal of the subsidy jeapordized nearly $500 million of unrated tax-exempt bonds sold for the projects.

Murphy, whose district includes Robbins, has said the incinerators were important to the predominantly black Chicago suburbs of Robbins and Ford Heights. He has also pointed out the repeal of the subsidy hurt the state's ability to sell bonds.
A spokesman for Clinton, N.J.-based Foster Wheeler Corp, whose Illinois subsidiary developed the Robbins incinerator, declined to comment on the bill.
Terry Colip, an equity developer in the Ford Heights facility, said he was hopeful for a legislative remedy.

Last year, CGE Ford Heights, the facility's developer, declared bankruptcy, triggering an event of default on its bonds. The facility was subsequently mothballed awaiting a resolution of the developers' lawsuit against Illinois officials.
"We're for anything that would get that plant going again," Colip said.

The bill may face a tough going in the General Assembly, which passed the repeal in a single day in January 1996. A top aide to Gov. Jim Edgar, who signed the repeal into law a year ago, has said it was "highly unlikely" the governor would change his mind about the subsidy.
Meanwhile, litigation challenging the lost subsidy is chugging along in court.

Steve Varick, a Chicago attorney representing state officials, said hearings on the state's motions to dismiss lawsuits brought by CGE Ford Heights and Fulton and by Foster Wheeler in Cook County Circuit Court could be heard next month.

While those two cases have been consolidated for pre-trial purposes, the Illinois Supreme Court has denied the state's motion to also consolidate a third lawsuit filed by Polsky Energy Corp., the developer of the Wood River facility. That lawsuit is pending in Madison County Circuit Court.

Varick also said that 10 environmental and public health groups, including the Sierra Club and the American Lung Association, have petitioned to file "friend of the court" briefs on behalf of the state in Cook County court.
